SysTickSystem Timer (SysTick)p. 120

SysTick at 0xE000E000

STCTRLSysTick Control and Status Registerp. 124

offset 0x010 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000004 · access RO, RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
16COUNTRO0Set when the counter has reached 0 since the register was last read; a read of STCTRL or any write to STCURRENT clears it. A debugger read through the DAP clears it only while MasterType in the AHB-AP Control Register is 0, and otherwise leaves it unchanged.
0No count to 0 since the last read.
1Counter has reached 0 since the last read.
2CLK_SRCRW1Selects the clock that drives the SysTick counter.
0PIOSC divided by 4.
1System clock.
1INTENRW0Enables the SysTick interrupt at count 0.
0No interrupt; software can poll COUNT to see whether the counter has reached 0.
1SysTick raises an interrupt to the NVIC on reaching 0.
0ENABLERW0Starts and stops the SysTick counter.
0Counter stopped.
1Counter runs repeatedly: it loads RELOAD, counts down, sets COUNT and raises the interrupt if INTEN is set on reaching 0, then reloads and counts again.

STRELOADSysTick Reload Value Registerp. 126

offset 0x014 · 32 bits · reset 0b00000000000000000000000000000000 · access RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
23:0RELOADRW0x0Start value copied into STCURRENT each time the counter reaches 0.

STCURRENTSysTick Current Value Registerp. 127

offset 0x018 · 32 bits · reset 0b00000000000000000000000000000000 · access RWC

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
23:0CURRENTRWC0x0Counter value at the moment of access; there is no read-modify-write protection. Any write clears it to 0 and also clears STCTRL.COUNT.

NVICNested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC)p. 120

NVIC at 0xE000E000

EN0Interrupt 0-31 Set Enablep. 128

offset 0x100 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31:0INTRW0x0One enable bit per interrupt, read to see which are enabled and written with 1 to enable; a bit is cleared only by writing 1 to the matching INT[n] bit of DISn.
0Read: interrupt disabled. Write: ignored.
1Read: interrupt enabled. Write: enables the interrupt.

PEND0Interrupt 0-31 Set Pendingp. 132

offset 0x200 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31:0INTRW0x0One pending bit per interrupt, read to see which are pending and written with 1 to make one pending; writing 1 to an already pending interrupt does nothing. A bit is cleared only by writing 1 to the matching INT[n] bit of UNPEND0.
0Read: interrupt not pending. Write: ignored.
1Read: interrupt pending. Write: makes the interrupt pending, even while it is disabled.

9DISOOFPRW0When set, floating-point instructions no longer complete out of order relative to integer instructions.

0DISMCYCRW0Stops load-multiple and store-multiple instructions being interrupted.
0No effect.
1LDM and STM are not interrupted; each must finish before the processor stacks state and enters a handler, which raises interrupt latency.

FAULTSTATConfigurable Fault Statusp. 163

offset 0xD28 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW1C

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
25DIV0RW1C0Usage fault from a divide by zero; the stacked return PC then points at the dividing instruction. The trap is enabled by CFGCTRL.DIV0. Write 1 to clear.
0No divide-by-zero fault, or the trap is off.
1An SDIV or UDIV ran with divisor 0.
24UNALIGNRW1C0Usage fault from an unaligned access; the trap is enabled by CFGCTRL.UNALIGNED. Unaligned LDM, STM, LDRD and STRD fault whatever the setting. Write 1 to clear.
0No unaligned access fault, or the trap is off.
1An unaligned memory access was made.
19NOCPRW1C0Usage fault from an attempt to access a coprocessor. Write 1 to clear.
0No coprocessor access fault.
1A coprocessor access was attempted.
18INVPCRW1C0Usage fault from an illegal load of the PC; the stacked return PC then points at the instruction that tried it. Write 1 to clear.
0No invalid PC load fault.
1An illegal EXC_RETURN load to the PC was attempted, from an invalid context or EXC_RETURN value.
17INVSTATRW1C0Usage fault from illegal use of the EPSR; the stacked return PC then points at the offending instruction. An undefined instruction using the EPSR does not set it. Write 1 to clear.
0No invalid state fault.
1An instruction made illegal use of the EPSR.
16UNDEFRW1C0Usage fault from an instruction the processor cannot decode; the stacked return PC then points at it. Write 1 to clear.
0No undefined instruction fault.
1An undefined instruction was attempted.
15BFARVRW1C0Set after a bus fault whose address is known; later faults, such as a memory management fault, can clear it. If a bus fault escalates to a hard fault by priority, the hard fault handler must clear it, so that a stacked active bus fault handler does not return to an overwritten FAULTADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0FAULTADDR does not hold a valid fault address.
1FAULTADDR holds a valid fault address.
13BLSPERRRW1C0Bus fault during floating-point lazy state preservation. Write 1 to clear.
0None occurred.
1A bus fault occurred during lazy state preservation.
12BSTKERW1C0Bus fault while stacking on exception entry. The SP is still adjusted, but the stacked context may be wrong, and no address goes to FAULTADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No stacking bus fault.
1Stacking on exception entry caused one or more bus faults.
11BUSTKERW1C0Bus fault while unstacking on exception return, chained to the handler: the original return stack remains, the SP is not adjusted, no new save is made and no address goes to FAULTADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No unstacking bus fault.
1Unstacking on exception return caused one or more bus faults.
10IMPRERW1C0Asynchronous data bus error; no address goes to FAULTADDR. If it is detected while the current priority is above the bus fault priority, the fault waits pending until all higher-priority work returns. A precise fault before the handler is entered leaves both IMPRE and a precise status bit set. Write 1 to clear.
0No imprecise data bus error.
1A data bus error occurred, and the stacked return address does not relate to the faulting instruction.
9PRECISERW1C0Precise data bus error; the fault address goes to FAULTADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No precise data bus error.
1A data bus error occurred, and the stacked return PC points at the faulting instruction.
8IBUSRW1C0Instruction bus error, detected at prefetch but flagged only when the processor tries to issue the faulting instruction; no address goes to FAULTADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No instruction bus error.
1An instruction bus error occurred.
7MMARVRW1C0Shows whether MMADDR holds a valid address. If a memory management fault escalates to a hard fault by priority, the hard fault handler must clear it, so that a stacked active memory management fault handler does not return to an overwritten MMADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0MMADDR does not hold a valid fault address.
1MMADDR holds a valid fault address.
5MLSPERRRW1C0Memory management fault during floating-point lazy state preservation. Write 1 to clear.
0None occurred.
1A memory management fault occurred during lazy state preservation.
4MSTKERW1C0Access violation while stacking on exception entry. The SP is still adjusted, but the stacked context may be wrong, and no address goes to MMADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No stacking memory management fault.
1Stacking on exception entry caused one or more access violations.
3MUSTKERW1C0Access violation while unstacking on exception return, chained to the handler: the original return stack remains, the SP is not adjusted, no new save is made and no address goes to MMADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No unstacking memory management fault.
1Unstacking on exception return caused one or more access violations.
1DERRRW1C0Data access violation; the stacked return PC points at the faulting instruction and the attempted address goes to MMADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No data access violation.
1A load or store was attempted where that operation is not allowed.
0IERRRW1C0Instruction access violation, raised by any access to an XN region even with the MPU off or absent; the stacked return PC points at the faulting instruction and no address goes to MMADDR. Write 1 to clear.
0No instruction access violation.
1An instruction fetch was attempted where execution is not allowed.

MPUCTRLMPU Controlp. 173

offset 0xD94 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW

  • Privileged access only. With ENABLE and PRIVDEFEN both set, privileged accesses outside enabled regions follow the default memory map and unprivileged ones raise a memory management fault.
  • Execute Never and Strongly Ordered rules apply to the System Control Space whatever ENABLE holds; with the MPU on, accesses to the System Control Space and the vector table are never blocked.
  • With ENABLE set, at least one region must be enabled for the system to run unless PRIVDEFEN is set; PRIVDEFEN set with no regions enabled lets only privileged software run.
  • With ENABLE clear, privileged and unprivileged accesses use the default memory map, as if no MPU were fitted.
  • Unless HFNMIENA is set, the MPU is off while handling an exception at priority -1 or -2 (hard fault, NMI, or with FAULTMASK set).
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
2PRIVDEFENRW0Lets privileged software fall back on the default memory map outside defined regions, treated as region -1 and outranked by every defined, enabled region; ignored while the MPU is off.
0With the MPU on, no background map: an access outside every enabled region faults.
1With the MPU on, privileged accesses outside enabled regions use the default map.
1HFNMIENARW0Keeps the MPU active inside the hard fault, NMI and FAULTMASK handlers; setting it with the MPU off gives unpredictable behaviour.
0MPU off in hard fault, NMI and FAULTMASK handlers whatever ENABLE holds.
1MPU on in hard fault, NMI and FAULTMASK handlers.
0ENABLERW0Turns the MPU on; with the MPU off and HFNMIENA set, behaviour is unpredictable.
0MPU off.
1MPU on.

LDOSPCTLLDO Sleep Power Controlp. 258

offset 0x1B4 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000018 · access RW

  • A write to VLDO leaves the LDO output unchanged whatever VADJEN holds; the output stays at its factory value.
  • LDO 1.2 V allows a system clock up to 80 MHz, 0.9 V up to 20 MHz; the PIOSC runs at 16 MHz at both.
  • If a debugger was attached at any point after the most recent power-on reset, the LDO keeps its voltage in Sleep and Deep-Sleep.
  • Leaving Sleep or Deep-Sleep takes 4 us longer when the LDO voltage has been adjusted.
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31VADJENRW0Lets VLDO set the LDO output voltage in Sleep.
0Factory default LDO voltage in Sleep; VLDO ignored.
1LDO voltage in Sleep set by VLDO.
7:0VLDORW0x18LDO output voltage code, used only while VADJEN is 1. A setting at or below the 1.2 V default is recommended for the lowest Sleep power.
0x120.90 V.
0x130.95 V.
0x141.00 V.
0x151.05 V.
0x161.10 V.
0x171.15 V.
0x181.20 V.
0x19-0xFFReserved.

  • Leaving Sleep or Deep-Sleep takes 4 us longer when the LDO voltage has been adjusted.

0No error.
1VLDO in LDOSPCTL or LDODPCTL asked for more than the maximum; the LDO goes to its factory default.

0No error.
1LDOSPCTL.VLDO below the minimum; the LDO voltage is left as is on entering Sleep.
3LDMINERRRO0Error: LDODPCTL.VLDO asked for an LDO voltage below the allowed minimum.
0No error.
1LDODPCTL.VLDO below the minimum; the LDO voltage is left as is on entering Deep-Sleep.
2PPDERRRO0Error: the PIOSC could not be turned off in Deep-Sleep as asked.
0No error.
1A PIOSC power-down for Deep-Sleep was asked for but is not possible; the PIOSC stays on in Deep-Sleep.

0No error.

FMPRE0Flash Memory Protection Read Enable 0p. 500

offset 0x130 · 32 bits · reset 0xFFFFFFFF · access RW

  • Covers flash 0 to 64 KB. Loaded at power-on reset; other resets leave it alone. Factory value is 1 in every implemented block, giving open access.
  • Bits can only go from 1 to 0. A cleared bit becomes permanent once committed; uncommitted, a power-on reset brings it back.
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31:0READ_ENABLERW0xFFFFFFFFOne bit per 2 KB flash block setting it read-only; combines with FMPPE0 into the block's protection policy.

offset 0x134 · 32 bits · reset 0xFFFFFFFF · access RW

  • Covers flash 0 to 64 KB. Loaded at power-on reset; other resets leave it alone. Factory value is 1 in every implemented block, giving open access.

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31:0PROG_ENABLERW0xFFFFFFFFOne bit per 2 KB flash block setting it execute-only; combines with FMPRE0 into the block's protection policy.

Setting it while an operation runs is ignored; it clears itself when the operation finishes.

offset 0x000 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
2:0GPTMCFGRW0x0Selects whether the timers run joined (32-bit, or 64-bit on a wide timer) or split into two halves (16-bit, or 32-bit on a wide timer); change only while GPTMCTL.TAEN and GPTMCTL.TBEN are both 0.
0x0Joined timer: 32-bit on a 16/32-bit timer, 64-bit on a 32/64-bit wide timer.
0x1Joined real-time clock counter: 32-bit on a 16/32-bit timer, 64-bit on a 32/64-bit wide timer.
0x2-0x3Reserved.
0x4Split timers: 16-bit each on a 16/32-bit timer, 32-bit each on a wide timer; each half's function is set by bits 1:0 of GPTMTAMR and GPTMTBMR.
0x5-0x7Reserved.

WDTCTLWatchdog Controlp. 701

offset 0x008 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RO, RW

  • A time-out can raise an interrupt, or a reset when the count expires a second time.
  • WDT1 runs from its own clock, so back-to-back writes, or a write then a read, to WDT1 registers need a gap; poll WRC for 1 before the next access. Back-to-back reads are unrestricted. WDT0 runs from the system clock and has no such limit.
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
31WRCRO1Write complete flag for WDT1: cleared by a write and set when that write has finished. On WDT0 the bit is reserved, with a reset value of 0.
0A WDT1 register write is still under way.
1No write under way; WDT1 registers may be accessed.
2INTTYPERW0Chooses whether the watchdog interrupt is ordinary or non-maskable.
0Standard interrupt.
1Non-maskable interrupt.
1RESENRW0Turns on the watchdog's reset output.
0Reset output off.
1Reset output on.
0INTENRW0Turns on the watchdog interrupt and starts the timer; once set, writes to it are ignored until a hardware reset or a software reset through SRWD.
0Interrupt off; after being set it clears only by hardware reset or an SRWD software reset.
1Interrupt on and timer running; further writes have no effect.

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
13:12SS3RW0x3Priority of Sample Sequencer 3, 0x0 highest to 0x3 lowest. Each sequencer needs a different value; equal values can make the ADC misbehave.

1:0SS0RW0x0Priority of Sample Sequencer 0, 0x0 highest to 0x3 lowest. Each sequencer needs a different value; equal values can make the ADC misbehave.

ADCDCCTL0ADC Digital Comparator Control 0p. 804

offset 0xE00 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RW

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
4CIERW0Turns on the comparison interrupt of this digital comparator.
0Comparison interrupt off; conversion data cannot raise it.
1Comparison interrupt on; conversion data raises it as CIC and CIM set.
3:2CICRW0x0Region, set by COMP0 and COMP1 in ADCDCCMPn, in which conversion data raises the interrupt.
0x0Low band: ADC data < COMP0 <= COMP1.
0x1Mid band: COMP0 <= ADC data < COMP1.
0x2Reserved.
0x3High band: COMP0 < COMP1 <= ADC data.
1:0CIMRW0x0How the comparison raises the interrupt.
0x0Always: interrupt on every conversion whose data lies in the chosen region.
0x1Once: interrupt only when the data first enters the chosen region.
0x2Hysteresis always: interrupt on every conversion in the chosen region until the data enters the opposite region, which clears the hysteresis.
0x3Hysteresis once: one interrupt when the data first lies in the chosen region, then none until the data enters the opposite region and clears the hysteresis.

CANCANp. 985

CAN0 at 0x40040000

CANCTLCAN Controlp. 987

offset 0x000 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000001 · access RW

  • Setting or clearing INIT does not shorten bus-off recovery. On going bus-off the controller sets INIT and all bus activity stops; once the CPU clears INIT it waits for 129 runs of 11 High bits (bus idle) before normal operation resumes, and the error counters are reset at the end. Each run of 11 High bits seen in that wait writes code 0x5 to CANSTS.LEC, so software can tell a bus stuck Low or disturbed and follow the recovery.
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
7TESTRW0Puts the CAN controller into test mode.
0Normal operation.
1Test mode.
6CCERW0Lets software write the CANBIT register.
0CANBIT cannot be written.
1CANBIT can be written while INIT is 1.
5DARRW0Turns off automatic resending of disturbed messages.
0Disturbed messages are resent automatically.
1No automatic resending.
3EIERW0Enables the error interrupt, raised by a change of CANSTS.BOFF or CANSTS.EWARN.
0No error interrupt.
1A change of BOFF or EWARN in CANSTS raises an interrupt.
2SIERW0Enables the status interrupt, raised by a change of CANSTS.TXOK, RXOK or LEC.
0No status interrupt.
1An interrupt follows each successful transmit or receive and each detected bus error, that is any change of TXOK, RXOK or LEC in CANSTS.
1IERW0Master enable for CAN interrupts.
0Disabled.
1Enabled.
0INITRW1Holds the controller in initialization; the controller sets it itself on going bus-off.
0Normal operation.
1Initialization begins.

CANSTSCAN Statusp. 989

offset 0x004 · 32 bits · reset 0x00000000 · access RO, RW

  • Reading CANSTS has side effects: it clears a pending CANINT. LEC is cleared when a message is sent or received without error; software may write the unused code 0x7 to LEC and watch for it to change. BOFF and EWARN raise the error interrupt, and RXOK, TXOK and LEC the status interrupt, when enabled in CANCTL; a change of EPASS or a write to RXOK, TXOK or LEC raises none.
BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
7BOFFRO0Shows whether the controller is bus-off.
0Not bus-off.
1Bus-off.
6EWARNRO0Shows that an error counter has reached the warning limit of 96.
0Both error counters under 96.
1One or both error counters at 96 or more.
5EPASSRO0Shows whether the module is error passive.
0Error active: receive or transmit error count at 127 or under.
1Error passive: receive or transmit error count over 127.
4RXOKRW0Set when a message has been received without error; software clears it by writing 0.
0No message received without error since the last clear.
1A message has been received without error since the last clear, whatever the acceptance filter decided.
3TXOKRW0Set when a message has been sent without error; software clears it by writing 0.
0No message sent without error since the last clear.
1A message has been sent without error and acknowledged by one or more other nodes since the last clear.
2:0LECRW0x0Code for the kind of error last seen on the CAN bus.
0x0No error.
0x1Stuff error: over 5 bits of the same level in a row where a received message forbids it.
0x2Format error: a fixed-format part of a received frame is malformed.
0x3ACK error: no other node acknowledged the sent message.
0x4Bit 1 error: sending a High (1), the controller read the bus as Low (0). Such a conflict counts as an error in every field but the arbitration field, where it is part of arbitration.
0x5Bit 0 error: the controller meant to send a Low (0) but read the bus as High (1); during bus-off recovery this code is set after every run of 11 High bits, so software can follow the recovery without disturbing the bus.
0x6CRC error: the CRC of a received message did not match the one computed.
0x7No event: no bus event since software wrote this code into LEC.

BitsFieldAccessResetWhat it does
14:12TSEG2RW0x2Phase 2 length after the sample point, in bit time quanta; the hardware uses the value plus 1, so the reset value 0x2 gives 3 quanta. Range 0x0 to 0x7; quantum set by BRP.
11:8TSEG1RW0x3Phase 1 length before the sample point, in bit time quanta; the hardware uses the value plus 1, so the reset value 0x3 gives 4 quanta. Range 0x0 to 0xF; quantum set by BRP.
7:6SJWRW0x0Amount, in bit time quanta, by which the controller can lengthen or shorten TSEG1 or TSEG2 when it sees a phase error at start of frame; the hardware uses the value plus 1, so reset 0 gives 1 quantum. Range 0x0 to 0x3.
5:0BRPRW0x1Divider from the CAN clock to the bit time quantum: the count of CAN clock periods in one quantum is the value plus 1 (reset gives 2). Range 0x00 to 0x3F; a bit time is a whole number of quanta; CANBRPE extends the divider.
